title: 2018 AMC 10B 21
statement: Mary chose an even \(4\)-digit number \(n.\) She wrote down all the divisors of \(n\) in increasing order from left to right: \(1,\) \(2,\) \(\ldots,\) \(\frac{n}{2},\) \(n.\) At some moment Mary wrote \(323\) as a divisor of \(n.\) What is the smallest possible value of the next divisor written to the right of \(323?\)

solutions.text:
Let \(d\) be the next divisor after \(323.\) If \(\gcd(d,323)=1,\) then \(n\) is a multiple of \(323d>323^2>9999,\) impossible for a four-digit number. Thus \(\gcd(d,323)>1.\)

Since \(323=17\cdot19,\) this gcd is at least \(17.\) It also divides \(d-323,\) so \(d-323\ge17\) and hence \(d\ge340.\)

This bound is attained: for \(n=6460=2^2\cdot5\cdot17\cdot19,\) both \(323\) and \(340\) are divisors. The lower bound shows there is no divisor between them. Thus the smallest possible next divisor is \(340,\) and C is the correct answer.
hints: \(323 = 17 \cdot 19,\) and \(n\) is an even \(4\)-digit multiple of \(323\)
For a candidate next divisor \(d,\) \(n\) must be a multiple of \(\operatorname{lcm}(323, d);\) find the smallest \(d > 323\) keeping that under \(10000\)
